The contract may impose a maximum notice period of no more than two months (Article 25(2)(d)). The transition itself must not exceed the mandatory maximum transitional period of 30 calendar days, initiated after the notice period (Article 25(2)(a)); if 30 days is technically unfeasible, the provider must notify the customer within 14 working days, justify this, and propose an alternative period of no more than seven months (Article 25(4)). The customer may also extend the transitional period once for a period it considers more appropriate (Article 25(5)). Switching charges may be imposed by the provider only in accordance with Article 29 (Article 25(2)(i)), typically covering costs like data egress or support actions (recital 88).

No — Article 18(c) requires that a data altruism organisation be legally independent from any entity operating on a for-profit basis, so a foundation legally controlled by a for-profit pharmaceutical group does not qualify. For a qualifying entity, once it has submitted all necessary information under Article 19(4) and the competent authority has evaluated the application and found it complies with Article 18, the authority must register it within 12 weeks after receipt of the application (Article 19(5)). That registration is valid in all Member States (Article 19(5)), and the Commission includes it in the public Union register.

Data Governance Act - definition: a legal person, including public sector bodies and international organisations, or a natural person who is not a data subject with respect to the specific data in question, which, in accordance with applicable Union or national law, has the right to grant access to or to share certain personal data or non-personal data.
Data Act - definition: a natural or legal person that has the right or obligation, in accordance with this Regulation, applicable Union law or national legislation adopted in accordance with Union law, to use and make available data, including, where contractually agreed, product data or related service data which it has retrieved or generated during the provision of a related service.

Both definitions allow a natural person to be a data holder, but the DGA restricts this to a natural person who is not a data subject with respect to the specific data in question, while the Data Act imposes no such restriction. The status is based on a right in both cases, but the DGA bases it on the right to grant access to or to share certain personal or non-personal data, whereas the Data Act bases it on the right or obligation to use and make available data, including product data or related service data retrieved or generated during the provision of a related service.
